title: Ramification and inertia
subject: galois
summary: Inertia describes the Galois action at ramified primes. An odd prime dividing a monic integer polynomial’s discriminant exactly once gives a transposition.
questionsAnswered: How do decomposition and inertia groups act on roots?
Why does discriminant valuation one give a transposition?
Why can a repeated reduction occur at an unramified prime?

sections.title: Decomposition and inertia groups
sections.body:
Let \(L/\mathbb Q\) be a finite Galois extension with group \(G\), and choose a prime \(\mathfrak P\) above \(p\). Its decomposition group \(D_{\mathfrak P}\) consists of automorphisms preserving \(\mathfrak P\). The inertia group \(I_{\mathfrak P}\) consists of those acting trivially on the residue field \(k_{\mathfrak P}=\mathcal O_L/\mathfrak P\). There is an exact sequence

\[1\longrightarrow I_{\mathfrak P}\longrightarrow D_{\mathfrak P}\longrightarrow\operatorname{Gal}(k_{\mathfrak P}/\mathbb F_p)\longrightarrow1.\]

Also \(D_{\mathfrak P}\cong\operatorname{Gal}(L_{\mathfrak P}/\mathbb Q_p)\). The local group is therefore a subgroup of the global Galois group. When \(p\) is unramified, inertia is trivial and residue Frobenius lifts uniquely inside \(D_{\mathfrak P}\). At a ramified prime it determines a coset modulo inertia. Inertia fixes the reductions of integral roots, while possibly permuting roots that collide.

citations.note: Exact sequence, maximal unramified subfield, and identification with the local Galois group.

sections.title: Tame inertia
sections.body:
In residue characteristic \(p\), inertia has a normal wild \(p\)-subgroup and a cyclic quotient of order prime to \(p\). If the extension is tame, wild inertia is trivial, so inertia itself is cyclic.

For irreducible \(f\), put \(K=\mathbb Q(\alpha)\). If its splitting field is tame at \(p\), write \(p\mathcal O_K=\prod_i\mathfrak p_i^{e_i}\), with residue degrees \(f_i\). A generator of inertia acts on the roots with an \(e_i\)-cycle repeated \(f_i\) times for each \(i\). Indeed, the decomposition orbit for \(\mathfrak p_i\) has size \(e_if_i\), and splits into \(f_i\) inertia orbits of size \(e_i\); a cyclic generator traverses each orbit. The integers \(e_i\) come from factorization in \(\mathcal O_K\). Repeated factors of \(f\bmod p\) can also arise from the index \([\mathcal O_K:\mathbb Z[\alpha]]\).

For example, \(x^3-5\) is Eisenstein over \(\mathbb Q_5\). Its root has valuation \(1/3\), forcing ramification index three. Adjoining a primitive cube root of unity is unramified at \(5\), since \(x^2+x+1\) has squarefree reduction. The splitting field therefore has cyclic inertia of order three, acting as a three-cycle. Here \(\Delta(x^3-5)=-675\) has valuation two at \(5\): tame inertia gives a 3-cycle although the discriminant valuation is not one.

sections.title: A simple discriminant prime
sections.body:
Theorem · simple discriminant prime

Let \(f\in\mathbb Z[x]\) be monic and separable, with splitting field \(L\). If \(p\) is odd and \(v_p(\Delta(f))=1\), then inertia at every prime of \(L\) above \(p\) has order two, and its nonidentity element acts as a transposition on the roots. Irreducibility is not required.

Proof

Multiplication by \(f'\) on the free \(\mathbb Z_p\)-module \(\mathbb Z_p[x]/(f)\) has determinant \(\operatorname{Res}(f,f')=\pm\Delta(f)\). Valuation one means its Smith normal form has exactly one nonunit diagonal entry, so reduction modulo \(p\) has cokernel dimension one. This cokernel is \(\mathbb F_p[x]/(\bar f,\bar f')\); hence \(\deg\gcd(\bar f,\bar f')=1\).

Since \(p\) is odd, necessarily \(\bar f=(x-a)^2\bar h\), where \(a\in\mathbb F_p\), \(\bar h\) is squarefree, and \(\bar h(a)\ne0\). Hensel's lemma lifts these coprime factors to \(f=qh\) over \(\mathbb Z_p\), with \(q\) quadratic. The identity

\[\Delta(f)=\Delta(q)\Delta(h)\operatorname{Res}(q,h)^2\]

and the unit factors \(\Delta(h)\) and \(\operatorname{Res}(q,h)\) give \(v_p(\Delta(q))=1\). The splitting field \(\mathbb Q_p(\sqrt{\Delta(q)})\) is ramified quadratic; the squarefree reduction of \(h\) makes its splitting field unramified. Their compositum therefore has inertia of order two, swapping precisely the two roots of \(q\).

citations.note: Hensel lifting and unramified extensions used in the explicit proof; the valuation-one deduction is supplied here.

citations.locator: Discriminant and Different, pp. 47–60; Ramification Groups, pp. 61–79

sections.title: Example
sections.body:
Example · \(x^3-x-1\)

The rational-root test proves \(f=x^3-x-1\) irreducible: neither \(1\) nor \(-1\) is a root. Its discriminant and bad-prime reduction are

\[\Delta(f)=-4(-1)^3-27(-1)^2=-23,\qquad f\equiv(x-10)^2(x-3)\pmod{23}.\]

Indeed, \(f-(x-10)^2(x-3)=23(x^2-7x+13)\). The theorem supplies an inertia transposition at \(23\). Since \(G\le S_3\) is transitive, \(3\mid |G|\); the transposition gives \(2\mid |G|\), so \(G=S_3\). The discriminant valuation proves nontrivial inertia; the repeated reduction alone would not suffice.

citations.note: Local-group background; all numerical identities and the elementary group argument are verified directly here.

sections.title: The index of an order
sections.body:
Remark

For monic irreducible \(f\) with root \(\alpha\) and \(K=\mathbb Q(\alpha)\),

\[\Delta(f)=\operatorname{disc}(K)\,[\mathcal O_K:\mathbb Z[\alpha]]^2.\]

Consider \(x^2-18\), with root \(3\sqrt2\). Modulo \(3\) it becomes \(x^2\), yet \(K=\mathbb Q(\sqrt2)\) has discriminant \(8\), so \(3\) is unramified and its inertia group is trivial. The polynomial discriminant is \(72=8\cdot3^2\): the repeated reduction comes from the index \(3\). If the polynomial discriminant has valuation one, the index is prime to \(p\).

A primitive subgroup containing a transposition is \(S_n\). Transitivity alone does not suffice.

citations.note: Index-squared discriminant identity and the ramification–discriminant criterion.

related.why: Squarefree reduction gives Frobenius cycle types; repeated reduction requires ramification and index information.
A simple discriminant prime isolates a ramified quadratic factor.
An inertia transposition and primitivity imply the full symmetric group.
Newton polygons constrain local factor degrees; inertia describes ramification permutations.

questions.title: Does a repeated root modulo p imply nontrivial inertia?
questions.body: No: \(x^2-18\) modulo \(3\) is a counterexample, because its root field is unramified at \(3\). The order index can account for repeated reduction; the valuation-one theorem excludes this obstruction.

citations.note: The published discriminant and ramification theory proves the distinction used in this counterexample.
Index-squared identity and the ramification criterion.
